summary: The note describes the New Testament as a collection of Christian works written in first-century Koine Greek by various writers, and notes its evolution into various Christian canons. It explains that the 27-book canon has been almost universally recognized since Late Antiquity, while some books were added or excluded over time. It also covers the dating of the original texts, which were written in the first and perhaps second centuries AD.
one_line: Overview of the New Testament's composition in first-century Koine Greek, its canonical development, and the dating of its books.
key_facts: The New Testament is a collection of Christian works written in the common (Koine) Greek language of the first century.
The modern consensus is that the New Testament provides important evidence regarding Judaism in the first century AD.
In almost all Christian traditions today, the New Testament consists of 27 books.
The twenty-seven-book canon of the New Testament, at least since Late Antiquity, has been almost universally recognized within Christianity.
Irenaeus of Lyon asserted the Canonical Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John as the Four Gospels in the late 2nd century.
Over time, disputed books such as the Book of Revelation and the Minor Catholic (General) Epistles were introduced into canons in which they were originally absent.
Works once held to be Scripture, such as 1 Clement, the Shepherd of Hermas, and the Diatessaron, were excluded from the New Testament.
The Old Testament canon is not completely uniform among Roman Catholics, Protestants, the Greek Orthodox Church, the Slavic Orthodox Churches, and the Armenian Orthodox Church.
Greek was the common language of the Eastern Mediterranean from the conquests of Alexander the Great (335-323 BC) until the Muslim conquests in the 7th century AD.
The original texts were written in the first and perhaps the second centuries of the Christian Era.
All works that eventually became part of the New Testament are believed to have been written no later than around 120 AD.
John A.T. Robinson, Dan Wallace, and William F. Albright dated all the books of the New Testament before 70 AD.
Some scholars give a final date of 80 AD for the New Testament books, or 96 AD.
A major collection of the letters of the Apostle Paul must have been made already by the early 2nd century.
